title: The storm (Acts 27:1–26)
hook: fourteen days without sun or stars, and an angel: fear not
tomorrow: a ship about to break apart. why talk about breakfast?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a king said almost, and Paul wished him everything except the chains. The line: except these chains.

A group project goes sideways, and suddenly the quiet one is keeping everybody calm. Acts 27 has a stranger version. A ship bound for Italy, a wind called Euroclydon, and "neither sun nor stars in many days appeared." The crew has thrown cargo overboard; Acts says "all hope that we should be saved was then taken away." The one who stands up with a pep talk isn't the captain. It's a prisoner, Paul. Odder still: he says the same words twice in four verses. Be of good cheer. Why twice?
screen: `THE QUIET ONE KEEPS EVERYONE CALM.` → `NO SUN, NO STARS, NO HOPE.` → `WHY SAY IT TWICE?`

segments.voice: Start with the first time. Paul opens with something very human, a small I-told-you-so: you should have listened to me and not sailed from Crete. Then: "And now I exhort you to be of good cheer: for there shall be no loss of any man's life among you, but of the ship." Big words from a man in chains. So he shows where they come from. An angel stood by him that night and said, "Fear not, Paul." Then the second time, and it's different: "Wherefore, sirs, be of good cheer: for I believe God, that it shall be even as it was told me." Here's the answer to the puzzle. The first good cheer points at the outcome: nobody dies. The second points at the ground under it: I believe God. Nothing outside changes between the two. The wind still howls. No sun, no stars. Paul's good cheer isn't a weather report. It rests on a promise, and he hands it to everyone on board, sailors, soldiers and prisoners alike. The storm still has days to run, until the fourteenth night.
screen: `I TOLD YOU SO, THEN GOOD CHEER.` · `FEAR NOT, PAUL.` · `SECOND TIME: I BELIEVE GOD.` · `NOT A WEATHER REPORT.` · then, large: `BE OF GOOD CHEER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a long storm, yours or someone's you love. Say the words out loud once, slowly: be of good cheer. Then hold them quietly through the sit, like a hand on a rope, and let the wind be what it is.
The storm. Days with no sun or stars, all hope gone, and a prisoner on his feet saying: be of good cheer.
The line to keep: be of good cheer, said in the middle of the storm, not after it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Christians turn to the storm stories of the Bible in hard seasons, and some keep a short line from scripture, such as be of good cheer or fear not, to hold onto in prayer.

fork.setup: a friend's family is in a long hard stretch with no end in sight. she asks you to just promise it'll be fine. what does Acts 27 suggest?
options: promise her the hard part will be over soon.
say the true thing you hold to, without faking the weather.
tell her cheer is pointless until things improve.
fork.reveal: Paul didn't say the storm would stop. he said what he believed, and why, while it was still dark.

original.note: Greek: be of good cheer, take heart. Paul's word to the ship in Acts 27:25.

trapdoor: what you thought: a shipwreck adventure.
what it means: a prisoner giving courage to a ship that had lost all hope, on the strength of a promise.
what a scholar hears: εὐθυμεῖν in 27:22 and εὐθυμεῖτε in 27:25, the same word twice, with the angel's message between.
guess: a long storm where Paul stood up and spoke courage
a storm Jesus calmed on the Sea of Galilee
the flood that Noah rode out in the ark
recall: every good thing, minus the bonds

chat.says: dad hurt his shoulder at a fire. surgery thursday. everyone keeps saying 'stay positive.' i can't fake it.
options: You don't have to fake it. Paul said good cheer with no sun out; hold one promise.
Then stay positive anyway. If you smile enough, the worry usually goes away.
Be honest that it's hopeless for now. Cheer only makes sense after the storm.
chat.meaning: Paul said be of good cheer with no sun or stars in sight. It rested on a promise, not on pretending the storm was over.

Euroclydon.meaning: the name Acts gives the storm wind

Crete.meaning: an island where the ship stopped before the storm
